Have your two weeks of tracking nearby. Your giving figures are personal. Take time to bring your decisions before God.
Here’s the strangest fundraising report in the Bible.
Paul is collecting money for Christians in Jerusalem who are going hungry. He writes to the church in Corinth, a wealthy port city, and tells them what happened up north in Macedonia.

Now, the Macedonian churches were poor. Paul’s phrase is “deep poverty”. They were also being persecuted. If we were drawing up a list of people to ask for money, we’d skip them and feel kind for doing it.

And Paul says: they begged us. They begged for the privilege of joining in. They gave what they could afford, and then more than they could afford. Out of severe trial and deep poverty came overflowing joy and a wealth of generosity.
Poverty, plus trouble, plus joy, equals generosity. No accountant alive would sign off on that sum. So how did it happen?
Something happened to them first
Paul tells us in his opening line. We want you to know about the grace of God given to the Macedonian churches.
He doesn’t say: let me tell you about some very impressive people. He says: let me tell you about grace. Something went into them before anything came out of them.
And a few verses later he says what it was. This is the centre of everything the Bible says about giving, so read it slowly.
You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich.
Slowly, then
He was rich. Think what the Son of God had. The love of the Father, from before time. The worship of heaven. Everything that exists was made through him and belonged to him.
He became poor. Born in a borrowed feeding trough. Nowhere to lay his head. And at the end, stripped. Soldiers rolled dice for the last thing he owned. He died owning nothing, carrying our sin.
For your sake. So that we, who had nothing to bring, might become rich. Forgiven. Adopted. Heirs of the world to come.
What Paul doesn’t do next
He doesn’t say: therefore, you owe ten percent. In verse 8 he says: I’m not commanding you. He refuses to. Giving that’s been squeezed out of someone isn’t what he’s after.
A chapter later he says it outright. Each person should give what they’ve decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

So let’s be as clear as Paul is. Nobody at Ev is going to pressure anyone to give. If giving feels like a bill, or a guilt trip, or the price of belonging, hear this: that isn’t Christianity. The gospel is free. Jesus paid.
But grace isn’t nothing
Grace does things to people. The Macedonians weren’t guilted. They were changed. They’d seen what Jesus gave up for them, and their grip came loose.

That’s why Paul keeps calling giving a grace, all the way through the chapter. And it’s why he says to the Corinthians, who were good at so many things: you excel in faith, in speech, in knowledge. See that you excel in this grace too.
Generosity is something we can get better at. Like prayer. Like knowing our Bibles. Nobody is born good at it.
Two questions to take into the passage

Do we know this grace? Not, do we know about it. Has the poverty of Jesus for us actually landed? Because when giving feels impossible, the fix is rarely a better budget. It’s a longer look at the cross.

And where’s the evidence? Paul says their giving would show their love was real. Grace that’s gone in comes out. If someone read our bank statements, would they find any sign that we’ve been loved like this?
Open 2 Corinthians 8 and read it together.

children.text: Pray first, on your own, for five minutes. Then work it out together.
Take five minutes to pray. Then think through the giving decision you would like to make.
Four questions to pray through first
Does this cost us anything? (2 Samuel 24:24)
Is it in proportion to what God has given us? (1 Corinthians 16:2)
Is the local church first? (Galatians 6:6)
Can we give this cheerfully? (2 Corinthians 9:7)
